instruction: SAFETY/BYPASS-lens R1 review of WP-SCP-022 slice 020M (supply-chain hash-pinning + v1.0.1 cut) at branch feature/wp-scp-022-020m-supply-chain-hashes, commit ee32abc. PR #84. PRIMARY THREAT MODEL FOR THIS SLICE: PyPI-supply-chain attack surface; lockfile-bypass paths; CI-time hash-check evasion. EXAMINE: (1) Hash-pin coverage gaps. The lockfile pins pyyaml==6.0.2 + jsonschema==4.23.0 + transitive deps (attrs, jsonschema-specifications, referencing, rpds-py). Are there ANY OTHER Python imports in the workflows that pip might satisfy from the runner's preinstalled site-packages or dynamically install — in particular, any 'import' statement in a python3 - <<PY heredoc that hits a package NOT in the lockfile. Look for: 'jsonschema.FormatChecker', 'jsonschema.Draft202012Validator', specific pyyaml safe_load options, etc. Are those covered by jsonschema/pyyaml respectively (no extra package needed)? Does any pip install in either workflow install something OTHER than via the lockfile (e.g. a different requirements file, or a new pip install command)? (2) Bypass via the conditional guard. Each policy-check.yml install site is 'if ! python3 -c import <pkg>; then pip install ...'. If a runner's environment has yaml/jsonschema preinstalled at the WRONG version (e.g. pyyaml 5.x or jsonschema 3.x), the import succeeds, the install is skipped, and the rest of the workflow runs against the wrong version. Is this a real risk? Check what pyyaml + jsonschema versions actions/runner-images ubuntu-latest preinstalls (if any). The 020M slice does not pin the *runtime version*; the pinning only triggers on install. (3) Path-traversal / injection risk. The install command uses ${SCP_RUNTIME_ROOT}/requirements/policy-check.txt. SCP_RUNTIME_ROOT is hardcoded at .scp-runtime via env: at job-level. Verify there is no way for an adopter to inject a different requirements file via inputs. SCP_RUNTIME_ROOT is not exposed via workflow_call.inputs. (4) The .scp-runtime symlink fallback (lines 107-113 of policy-check.yml). When SCP self-call hits the symlink fallback, .scp-runtime is symlinked to $(pwd) — the caller's working directory. If the caller is SCP itself (self-call), the requirements file at .scp-runtime/requirements/policy-check.txt resolves to the same file as the caller's checkout. Verify this is correct AND secure (an attacker controlling the caller cannot substitute a different requirements file because the SHA-pin enforcement on the wrapper IS the trust root for this path). (5) release-gate.yml: requirements/policy-check.txt is read from the SCP repo's own checkout (line 100 actions/checkout). No adopter can influence this path. (6) D-038 ratification: the decision row should be a privilege-write expansion ratification (SHOULD be like D-029 / D-037 — it's not, because it's not a privilege expansion; it's a hardening). Verify D-038's framing is internally coherent (PATCH bump for internal hardening; not a permission/privilege change). (7) Version-pin staleness in the lockfile. attrs==26.1.0, jsonschema-specifications==2025.9.1, referencing==0.37.0, rpds-py==0.30.0 — these are the LATEST at pip-compile time. Are these versions safe (no known CVEs)? Spot-check the rpds-py version is recent enough to not have the known C-extension memory corruption issue. (8) Renovate cascade: when v1.0.1 is published, Renovate adopters get auto-bumped. Does the bump PR fail closed if anything in the new requirements/policy-check.txt is unverifiable? The hash-pin makes pip refuse install, which makes the workflow fail with SCP-E001 — adopter sees red CI. This is the desired behaviour. Verify there is no 'pin to latest' or 'bypass --require-hashes via env' path. (9) Lockfile regeneration social-engineering: the pip-compile command is documented in .in + .txt headers; an attacker who edits .in and pushes a PR could substitute different transitive versions. Is this attack mitigated by CODEOWNERS coverage on requirements/**? CHECK CODEOWNERS for the path and report if not covered. (10) Cross-workflow drift: if a future PR bumps pyyaml in policy-check.yml's inline pin (not via the lockfile) without updating release-gate.yml, the two would drift. Since this slice removes the inline pins from policy-check.yml entirely (replaced with a lockfile reference), and release-gate.yml is also lockfile-only, this risk is eliminated FOR THIS WP. But if a future operator re-adds an inline pip install --user pkg==ver to either workflow, the drift would silently bypass the lockfile. Is there guard rail (e.g. workflow-selftest checking for inline pip installs)? Identify if not. (11) workflow_selftest: does it install python deps via the same lockfile or a different mechanism? If different, the selftest may not exercise the hash-pinned path. (12) `gh attestation verify` was discussed in TF-007 as soft-warn for OPA. The 020M slice does NOT add `gh attestation verify` for pip-installed wheels; this is a known gap (PyPI doesn't publish Sigstore attestations either). Verify that the slice doesn't claim hash-pin == attestation-equivalent (the lockfile is hash-pinned, not signature-attested). Per WP-SCP-022 §4.3. Return SonnetReviewResult JSON. NEVER recommend descoping.
